rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify poorly resolved pairs while retaining early compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the unresolved pair responds to a shallower slope. This also measures the retention-time tradeoff before trimming the gradient window or changing temperature.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward while keeping the slope close to injection 2, which resolved every pair. This should remove roughly a minute of low-organic delay and bring the last peak below 10 minutes while preserving resolution.
Slightly reduce the gradient slope to raise the critical pair from R = 1.42 above 1.5. The last peak is predicted to remain near, but just below, 10 minutes, targeting the maximum CRF of 1.0.

Increase the slope only slightly from injection 4, targeting a last peak strictly below 10 minutes while retaining the critical pair above R = 1.5. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.
Injection 5 achieved the maximum CRF; now increase only temperature to seek a shorter fully resolved run. This isolates temperature's effect on the critical pair while preserving the proven gradient.

Test whether the critical pair separates again after a temperature-induced elution-order reversal, while shortening retention further. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate selectivity changes and check for new limiting pairs.

Shorten the fully resolved 55 C method by steepening the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed. The reversed critical pair may gain separation with increasing slope; this run will also check whether another pair becomes limiting.

Raise both gradient endpoints equally to reduce low-organic delay while preserving the slope of injection 8. Check whether the early peaks remain retained and the two marginal pairs stay fully resolved in a shorter run.

Explore a faster, hotter gradient to test whether the newly limiting pair separates after an elution-order reversal. Restore phi0 to 0.10 to protect early-peak retention; injection 8 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Return to 55 C and lower the starting organic fraction to improve separation of the pair that worsened when phi0 increased. An eight-minute gradient tests whether that selectivity gain permits a faster fully resolved run than injection 8.

Reduce the slope from injection 11 to improve its limiting pair while retaining the low starting organic fraction. This targets full resolution with a last peak around 7.5 minutes, slightly faster than injection 8.

Test whether raising the organic window separates the reversed limiting pair from injection 10 while preserving its fast gradient slope. Monitor early-peak retention and neighboring pairs; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Use a steeper gradient to increase separation of the reversed pair seen at 60 C, while lowering phi0 to protect its neighboring pair and early peaks. This tests a faster selectivity regime rather than further compressing the starting window.

Explore the untested low-temperature selectivity regime using the original scouting gradient. Cooling may resolve the original critical pair, but the full table will reveal whether other pairs cross or become limiting before attempting a faster low-temperature method.

Test an intermediate temperature between the crowded 25 C result and the nearly resolved 40 C scout, keeping the gradient unchanged. This checks for a useful lower-temperature selectivity window while retaining the confirmed maximum-CRF methods as fallbacks.

Return to the successful 40 C selectivity regime with a slightly shallower gradient to strengthen the critical separation. Raising phi0 should offset the added retention, targeting full resolution below 10 minutes with more margin than injection 5.

Test the unexamined 50 C selectivity regime with a fast gradient, seeking a shorter fully resolved method. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention, while the temperature change may separate the pairs limiting the fast 60 C runs.

Seek a more robust maximum-CRF method near injection 12 by slightly reducing gradient slope. This should improve the marginal fourth–fifth separation while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes; the other critical pair will be checked for any loss of resolution.

Combine the higher starting organic fraction, which improved one critical pair in injection 9, with a shallower slope to recover its other limiting pair. This targets a maximum-CRF method with better resolution margins while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten the gradient from the fully resolved injection 8 to improve its limiting pair while preserving the favorable starting composition. This targets greater resolution margin for both critical pairs with the last peak still comfortably below 10 minutes.

Flatten injection 20's gradient further to bring its limiting pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the stronger separation of the other critical pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, targeting maximum CRF with improved resolution margins.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 22 to shorten retention while retaining its improved critical-pair margins. The predicted minimum resolution remains above 1.5, targeting another maximum-CRF method with a last peak near 9 minutes.
Use a gradient slope midway between injections 8 and 21 to balance their two critical separations. This targets maximum CRF with a minimum resolution around 1.58 and a last peak near 8 minutes.

Preserve injection 12's successful gradient slope through the critical peak cluster, then hold at 50% organic. This tests a shorter programmed gradient with lower solvent demand; the last peak may elute somewhat later during the hold, but should remain below 10 minutes.
